atom.desc: The craft of building classifications that carve a domain at its joints — taxonomies, ontologies, coordinate systems where placement has a defensible answer

living-abstract.essence: The craft of structuring a domain into a classification — a taxonomy, ontology, or coordinate system that carves the space at its natural joints. The artifact is the map by which things in a domain are placed, named, and related: the structure that turns a flat pile into a navigable space.
living-abstract.purpose: Build classifications that reveal structure rather than impose it — where every category earns its existence, boundaries fall at real seams, and "where does this go?" has a defensible answer rather than a guess. The instrument by which a population of things becomes a system.
living-abstract.capacity: Find the joints — the dimensions and boundaries that are real in the domain, so categories are discovered, not invented for tidiness.
Decide depth by meaning — add a level only when it tells you something its parent and children do not; refuse the level that exists merely to file.
Recognize when items vary along independent dimensions and split them into orthogonal axes rather than forcing one hierarchy to carry them all.
living-abstract.principle: A good classification reflects real structure in the domain; its categories are discovered by asking what genuinely distinguishes one thing from another. Aim for mutually exclusive, jointly exhaustive where the domain allows it — a thing belongs in one place, and every thing has a place.

A category exists only if it carries meaning its parent and children do not. The semantic-value test is the single gate on depth: a level that only groups is a filing cabinet, and filing is debt, not structure. Depth is earned, never spent on neatness.

When items vary along independent dimensions, those are separate axes, not deeper nesting. Cross-classification (faceted) composes multiplicatively and stays shallow; forcing orthogonal facets into a single tree produces duplication and dead branches.

living-concrete.knowledge: Three structures, each fitting a different domain shape: a **hierarchy** (tree) when items genuinely nest — one dimension, parent contains child. A **faceted** scheme (multiple independent axes) when items vary along dimensions that do not nest — coordinates, not a single path; this is the more powerful default and the one most often missed. A **flat** list when the population is small and undifferentiated, and any structure would be overhead. The error is reaching for a hierarchy by reflex when the domain is faceted.
living-concrete.pattern: When an item is hard to place — it seems to belong in two branches at once — the taxonomy is telling you something, not failing. Usually the item spans two orthogonal dimensions that the structure has collapsed into one. The fix is rarely "pick a branch"; it is to split the conflated dimension into separate axes and let the item take a coordinate on each.
living-concrete.antipattern: A category that groups its children but adds no meaning of its own — "miscellaneous", "languages", "general". It fails the semantic-value test: remove it and nothing is lost but a click of depth. The smell is a level you created to tidy the list rather than to express a distinction. Cure: flatten it, or find the real dimension it was pretending to be.
